skills.name: Support ticket triage
skills.one_liner: Categorize, prioritize and route a ticket backlog with suggested replies.
skills.description: Triages a ticket backlog against a contact-reason taxonomy using impact x urgency and SLA age. Safety, legal-threat, privacy-request and fraud tickets are flagged and routed, suggested replies are drafted for the top reasons, and tags and routing are written back only after approval. No customer is messaged by this skill.
skills.when: the support inbox has piled up, after a weekend, holiday or incident, or the team can't tell what to answer first

inputs.label: Open tickets with subject, body, channel, customer, age and history
Existing contact-reason categories and SLAs
Who handles what
Existing macros and help articles

outputs.name: Triaged backlog
outputs.description: Ticket, reason, sentiment, priority, SLA status, flag, route, confidence and suggested macro.

outputs.name: Suggested replies
outputs.description: Drafts for the top five reasons, for agents to edit and send.

outputs.name: Backlog report
outputs.description: Volume by reason, oldest tickets, SLA breaches, repeat contacts and upstream causes.

skills.instructions: 1. Pull open tickets (subject, body, channel, customer tier, age, previous contacts) with connector_read. Mask payment details and any personal data not needed for triage. 2. Reuse the existing contact-reason taxonomy, or propose a two-level one with 10–25 reasons. 3. Classify each ticket in code_interpreter with embeddings_search support: reason, sentiment, urgency, customer value and confidence. Prioritise with impact x urgency and SLA age. 4. Flag must-escalate tickets: safety issues; legal threats or regulator complaints; privacy requests (access or deletion, routed to the privacy owner with their deadline); chargebacks or fraud; VIPs; and anything the customer calls a complaint. 5. Route each ticket to an owner or queue with a reason. 6. Draft suggested replies for the top five reasons from existing macros and help articles. These are drafts for agents to edit and send. 7. Raise the write-back batch with request_owner_decision; only after approval write tags, priority and assignment with connector_write, keeping receipts. No customer-facing message is sent. 8. Report volume by reason, the oldest tickets, SLA breaches, repeat contacts and the upstream causes to fix. 9. State what could not be verified: low-confidence classifications and tickets needing account data the connector can't read.

workflow.brief: Read open tickets and history from the help desk.
workflow.acceptance: All open tickets loaded, with counts per channel.

workflow.title: Classify and prioritise
workflow.brief: Classify reason, sentiment, urgency and value, and prioritise.
workflow.acceptance: Each ticket has reason, priority and confidence; low-confidence ones are flagged.

workflow.title: Suggested replies
workflow.brief: Draft replies for the top five reasons from macros and KB.
workflow.acceptance: Each draft is linked to its reason and source macro or article.

workflow.title: Escalation and accuracy check
workflow.brief: Check flags and a sample of classifications.
workflow.acceptance: First line is APPROVED or CHANGES; all safety, legal and privacy tickets flagged; sample accuracy at least 90%.

workflow.title: Approve write-back
workflow.brief: The owner approves tags and routing changes.
workflow.acceptance: Approval recorded for the batch.

workflow.title: Write tags and routing
workflow.brief: Write approved tags, priority and assignment to the help desk.
workflow.acceptance: Receipt shows updated tickets; no customer-facing message sent.

No reply is sent to customers by this skill

skills.name: Support macro library
skills.one_liner: Reusable, on-voice replies for the top contact reasons.
skills.description: Builds reusable, on-voice support replies (macros) for the contact reasons that make up most volume. Each one is learned from real resolved tickets and checked against current written policy: answer first, clear next step and timing, variables with fallbacks, an internal note for agents, and a KB link. Imported to the help desk only after approval.
skills.when: agents answer the same questions differently, handle times are high, or a new agent is joining

inputs.label: Last 90 days of resolved tickets
Current returns, shipping, billing and service policies
Voice and tone guide
Current saved replies

outputs.name: Macro library
outputs.description: One macro per reason with variables, internal note, tags and KB link.

outputs.name: Macro index
outputs.description: Reason, volume share, macro name, tags, policy reference and last-reviewed date.

skills.instructions: 1. Rank contact reasons by volume over the last 90 days with connector_read and code_interpreter, and target the top 15–25 (usually 70–80% of volume). 2. For each reason, read at least ten real resolved tickets to learn the actual resolution and what customers ask next. 3. Load the voice and tone guide and the current policies with memory_recall; flag policy gaps or contradictions to the owner rather than papering over them. 4. Write each macro: a brief, human opening (no scripted over-apology), the answer first, numbered steps, what happens next and when, and one question to confirm resolution. Add variables for name, order and dates with safe fallbacks, and an internal note for agents (when not to use it, what to check first). 5. Write in plain language, avoid jargon and blame, and keep formatting accessible (short paragraphs, never image-only instructions). Link to KB articles where they exist. 6. QA each macro against written policy and against three real tickets. 7. Raise the import with request_owner_decision; only after approval create the macros in the help desk with connector_write, named and tagged consistently. 8. State what could not be verified: policies that aren't written down and reasons with fewer than ten examples.

skills.one_liner: Task-based help articles written from real tickets, KCS-style.
skills.description: Writes task-based help articles from real tickets using Knowledge-Centered Service: the title and problem in the customer's own words, environment, one-action numbered steps validated against the current product, annotated screenshots with alt text, and metadata with an owner and review date. Published to the help centre only after owner approval.
skills.when: the same question keeps coming in, help-centre searches return nothing, or an article is out of date

Screenshots or a walkthrough of the current product
Help-centre style and voice guide

outputs.name: Help article
outputs.description: Title, issue, environment, steps, cause, related articles, with alt text on images.

outputs.name: Annotated screenshots
outputs.description: Click targets highlighted per step.

outputs.name: Article backlog
outputs.description: Other gaps found, ranked by ticket volume.

skills.instructions: 1. Find candidates with connector_read and embeddings_search: top contact reasons without an article, help-centre searches with no results, and poorly rated articles. 2. Read five to ten real tickets per topic and capture the customer's own words for the title and problem statement (KCS: capture in the workflow, structure for reuse). 3. Structure the article: a title naming the task or problem in customer language ('Change the delivery address on an order'); the issue; the environment (plan, device, app version); numbered resolution steps, one action each; the cause if useful; related articles. 4. Capture screenshots (owner-provided or from a product walkthrough), read them with vision_describe, highlight click targets with image_edit, and write alt text for each. 5. Write in plain language: second person, present tense, roughly eighth-grade reading level, UI labels in bold exactly as they appear. 6. Validate by following the steps against the current product (or have a coworker do it). 7. Add metadata: tags, audience, owner and last-reviewed date. Render with web_page_generate. 8. Publish to the help centre with publish_external only after owner approval via request_owner_decision; link it from the relevant macros and set a review date. 9. State what could not be verified: steps not tested on every plan, device or app version.

skills.name: CSAT & NPS driver analysis
skills.one_liner: What drives satisfaction and detraction, with fixes ranked by impact.
skills.description: Explains what drives CSAT, NPS or CES. Each metric is computed to its standard definition with confidence intervals and cut by segment and touchpoint. Verbatims are coded, themes and operational data are linked to scores in a key-driver analysis, and fixes are ranked by impact and effort. Small samples are flagged, and correlation is never presented as causation.
skills.when: a satisfaction score dropped or plateaued, before planning, or when the owner asks 'why are customers unhappy?'

inputs.label: Survey responses with score, comment, date, channel and segment
inputs.example: NPS export from the survey tool

inputs.label: Linked tickets, orders, delivery times or usage
Previous periods' results

outputs.name: Driver analysis report
outputs.description: Scores with intervals, themes, drivers, segment cuts and ranked fixes.

outputs.name: Coded responses and driver model
outputs.description: Every response coded; driver model with method and sample sizes.

outputs.name: Driver impact chart
outputs.description: Themes by effect on score and share of respondents.

skills.instructions: 1. Pull responses (score, comment, date, channel, segment) and linked ticket, order or usage data with connector_read or file_parse; note response rates. 2. Compute each metric to its standard definition in code_interpreter: NPS = % promoters (9–10) minus % detractors (0–6); CSAT = % scoring 4–5 on a 5-point scale; CES as the mean. Give confidence intervals and never compare segments under n=30. 3. Code comments against a codebook (theme, sentiment, touchpoint), with embeddings_search proposing clusters and a close reading refining them. Report themes as % of respondents. 4. Run a key-driver analysis relating themes and operational data (resolution time, contacts to resolve, delivery delay) to scores: regression or relative importance, or simple lift tables for small samples. 5. Cut by channel, product, team and customer tenure, and trend over time with control bands. 6. Rank fixes by effect on score x number of customers affected ÷ effort, separating quick wins from systemic fixes. 7. List detractors who asked for follow-up so the team can contact them; nobody is contacted automatically. 8. State what could not be verified: non-response bias and causal claims from correlational data.

workflow.brief: Read survey responses and linked operational data.
workflow.acceptance: Response count, response rate and period recorded.

workflow.title: Scores and intervals
workflow.brief: Compute metrics with intervals by segment.
workflow.acceptance: Standard definitions used; segments under n=30 flagged.

workflow.title: Code verbatims
workflow.brief: Code comments into themes.
workflow.acceptance: Every comment coded; themes as % of respondents.

workflow.title: Driver analysis
workflow.brief: Relate themes and operational data to scores.
workflow.acceptance: Method and sample size stated for each driver.

workflow.title: Findings and fix list
workflow.brief: Render report, coded data and chart.
workflow.acceptance: Fixes ranked by impact and effort.

workflow.title: Statistical honesty review
workflow.brief: Check comparisons, sample sizes and causal language.
workflow.acceptance: First line is APPROVED or CHANGES; no segment comparisons under n=30; correlation not presented as causation.

quality_checks.criterion: Metrics use the standard definitions, with confidence intervals
Small samples are flagged and no comparisons are made under n=30

skills.one_liner: Milestones to first value with checklists, emails and success criteria.
skills.description: Designs onboarding to first value. The activation milestone is defined from retention data, and the current journey is mapped with its waits and drop-offs. Output includes stage checklists with exit criteria for customer and team, paths by segment, a welcome sequence, a kickoff agenda and risk triggers with playbooks.

skills.instructions: 1. Define 'first value' with data in code_interpreter: which early actions predict retention (for example, customers who do X within 14 days retain twice as well). Agree the activation milestone and a target time-to-value. 2. Map the current journey from purchase or contract to first value with diagram_generate: steps, owners, wait times and drop-offs. 3. Design the stages (welcome and kickoff, setup, training, first value, habit and expansion), each with customer tasks, our tasks, a checklist and exit criteria. 4. Set paths by segment: high-touch, low-touch and tech-touch by account value and complexity. 5. Write the welcome sequence timed to stages, one action per message, plus a kickoff agenda (goals, success criteria, roles, timeline) and a training outline. 6. Define risk triggers (no login by day 3, setup incomplete by day 10) and a playbook for each. 7. Set metrics: time to first value, activation rate, onboarding CSAT and early churn. 8. State what could not be verified: activation correlations from small cohorts.

skills.name: Churn risk review
skills.one_liner: Health signals, at-risk accounts and a save play for each.
skills.description: Reviews account health using usage, support, billing and relationship signals, weighted by how well each predicted past churn. It ranks at-risk accounts by risk x value with specific evidence for each, a churn-reason hypothesis and a tailored save play within approved limits, and names the systemic drivers to fix upstream.
skills.when: renewals are coming up, revenue retention is slipping, or the owner senses customers are quietly leaving

inputs.label: Usage, tickets, billing, NPS and contract data per account
Accounts that churned and when
What the team may offer to save an account
inputs.example: Up to one free month or a downgrade

outputs.name: Health scores and at-risk list
outputs.description: Signals, validated weights, score, risk x value rank and evidence per account.

outputs.name: Save plays per account
outputs.description: Reason hypothesis, play, owner, date and message angle.

outputs.name: Health distribution and churn drivers
outputs.description: Where risk sits and why.

skills.instructions: 1. Pull signals per account with connector_read: usage trend (logins, key actions, seats), support tickets and sentiment, billing (failed payments, downgrades, discount expiries), relationship (champion left, no executive contact, NPS) and contract (renewal date, term). 2. Build or refresh a health score in code_interpreter, with weights validated against past churn: compare churned and retained accounts and show each signal's lift. Drop signals that did not predict. 3. Rank accounts by risk x value and list the top at-risk ones with specific evidence (for example 'usage down 60% since the champion left in May'). 4. Assign each a churn-reason hypothesis: value not realised, poor fit, budget, competitor, service failure or champion loss. 5. Write a save play per account (re-onboarding, executive sponsor call, success-plan reset, right-sized offer within the owner's limits) with an owner, date and message angle. 6. Summarise the systemic drivers across accounts and the upstream fixes. 7. State what could not be verified: accounts with missing signals and weak predictive power where past churn is small.

skills.one_liner: A QBR deck that proves value, surfaces risks and proposes next steps.
skills.description: Builds a quarterly business review deck that proves value against the customer's own goals, with the calculation shown. It covers what worked and what didn't and what we're doing about it, and proposes next-quarter goals and a mutual action plan. It comes with speaker notes, a customer pre-read and an internal prep page.

skills.instructions: 1. Recall the customer's success plan with memory_recall: goals and success metrics set at onboarding or at the last QBR. 2. Pull usage, outcomes, support history and billing with connector_read. Compute value in the customer's terms (hours saved, revenue, cost reduction, service levels) in code_interpreter, showing the calculation and using customer-validated inputs where possible. 3. Storyline for 8–12 slides: goals recap; results against goals; what worked; what didn't and what we're doing about it; roadmap fit; recommendations; next-quarter goals and a mutual action plan. 4. Be honest about misses. A QBR that only brags loses trust. 5. Propose expansion only where it serves a goal the customer stated; no hard sell. 6. Build charts with chart_generate, takeaway in the title. Use the customer's logo only with permission. 7. Build the deck with deck_generate with speaker notes, and a one-page pre-read to send two days before. 8. Write an internal prep page: risks, stakeholders, asks and walk-away points. 9. State what could not be verified: value estimates that rest on assumptions.

skills.name: Escalation & complaint response
skills.one_liner: HEARD-based reply, remedy options and a root-cause hand-off.
skills.description: Handles an escalated complaint. It builds the full history, assesses severity and legal or safety implications, and drafts a HEARD reply (Hear, Empathise, Apologise, Resolve, Diagnose) with a proportional remedy from the remedy matrix. The root cause is handed off with evidence and a follow-up is set. The reply is sent once, only after owner approval.
skills.when: a customer is angry, has escalated, threatened to leave or post publicly, or a complaint has bounced between people

inputs.label: All tickets, orders, calls and public posts about the case
What remedies are allowed and up to what value
Anything the owner knows that records don't show
Voice and tone guide

outputs.name: HEARD reply
outputs.description: Short, specific, human reply with remedy and timing.

outputs.name: Case summary and remedy decision
outputs.description: Timeline, severity, flags, remedy options and recommendation.

outputs.name: Root-cause hand-off note
outputs.description: What went wrong upstream, with evidence, for the owning team.

skills.instructions: 1. Read the full history with connector_read (tickets, orders, calls, public posts) and build a timeline of what happened and what the customer was told. 2. Assess severity, public visibility and customer value. Legal threats, injury or safety issues, discrimination claims and regulator complaints go to the owner (and, where needed, a licensed professional) before any reply. 3. Draft the reply with HEARD: Hear (restate their experience specifically), Empathise, Apologise for what we got wrong without admitting legal liability or blaming staff, Resolve (the concrete remedy and its timing), Diagnose (what we're changing so it doesn't recur). 4. Choose a remedy from the remedy matrix (refund, replacement, credit, service-recovery gesture) proportional to the impact; anything beyond the limits goes to the owner via request_owner_decision. 5. Suggest a phone call for high-emotion cases, and keep the written reply short and human. 6. Hand the root cause to the operations or product owner with message_coworker, including the evidence. 7. Set a follow-up date and what will be confirmed. 8. Send only after owner approval, exactly once, with send_external, keeping the receipt. 9. State what could not be verified: claims the customer made that records don't show.

skills.name: Voice-of-customer report
skills.one_liner: Themes from tickets, reviews and surveys with verbatims and asks.
skills.description: Turns tickets, reviews, surveys, call notes and public posts into one voice-of-customer report. Everything is coded with a single codebook and themes are ranked by unique customers, with the source mix shown. Verbatims are de-identified, each theme becomes an ask with an owner and evidence, last period's asks are tracked, and an audio highlight reel is added.
skills.when: before quarterly planning, after a launch, or when teams argue about what customers want

inputs.label: Tickets, reviews, survey comments, call notes and community posts for the period
Period to cover
Last period's asks and their status

outputs.name: VOC report
outputs.description: Ranked themes, trends, de-identified verbatims and asks per team.

outputs.name: Coded feedback
outputs.description: Every item with source, date, codes and theme.

outputs.name: Customer voices highlight reel
outputs.description: Verbatims read aloud, labelled as customer quotes read by AI voices.

outputs.name: Theme trends
outputs.description: Themes over time by source.

skills.instructions: 1. Gather sources for the period with connector_read and file_parse (tickets, reviews, survey comments, call notes and transcripts, community posts) plus public mentions via x_search. Record volume per source. 2. De-identify: remove names, emails, order numbers and other identifiers from anything quoted. 3. Code everything with one codebook across sources (theme, sub-theme, sentiment, journey stage, segment), with embeddings_search proposing clusters and reading refining them. 4. Rank themes in code_interpreter by reach (unique customers), severity and trend against last period, and show the source mix so one loud channel doesn't dominate. 5. Pick two or three verbatims per theme, de-identified, with source type and date. 6. Turn themes into asks, each with an owner team, the evidence, a suggested action and the expected impact; report the status of last period's asks. 7. Render a three-to-five-minute highlight reel with tts, clearly labelled as customer quotes read by AI voices. 8. State what could not be verified: gaps in source coverage and sampling bias towards people who complain.

skills.name: Save & cancellation flow
skills.one_liner: Respectful cancellation flow with reasons capture and fair save offers.
skills.description: Designs a respectful save-and-cancel flow: cancellation as easy as sign-up, one reason question, reason-matched offers (pause, downgrade, fix) that are capped and modelled, an equal-prominence 'cancel anyway', and a clear confirmation. A win-back sequence respects unsubscribes. It is prototyped in the canvas, reviewed for dark patterns, and auto-renewal law is flagged for counsel.
skills.when: cancelling is hard or impossible online, churn is high, or the owner wants to save customers without trapping them

inputs.label: Cancellations with reasons, tenure, plan and past save outcomes
How cancelling works today
Discounts, pauses or downgrades the owner will allow
Where subscribers are

outputs.name: Cancellation flow prototype
outputs.description: Clickable flow from entry to confirmation.

outputs.name: Flow spec and copy
outputs.description: Screens, reason list, offer rules, confirmation content and metrics.

outputs.name: Offer economics
outputs.description: Save-rate assumptions, discount cost, retained LTV and cannibalisation.

outputs.name: Confirmation and win-back emails
outputs.description: Confirmation with end date and data export, and a 30/60/90-day win-back.

skills.instructions: 1. Pull cancellation data with connector_read: volumes, stated reasons, tenure, plan, and which saves have worked. 2. Principle: cancelling must be as easy as signing up. No obstruction, confirmshaming, hidden links or forced calls; dark patterns destroy trust and can breach consumer law. 3. Design the flow: a one-click entry; one reason question (six to eight reasons plus 'other'); a reason-matched offer (pause for 'not using it right now', downgrade for 'too expensive', help or fix for 'not working', none for 'moving or closing'); a 'cancel anyway' button of equal prominence; and a confirmation screen and email with end date and data export. 4. Model offer economics in code_interpreter: save-rate assumptions, discount cost, retained LTV and cannibalisation (people who would have stayed anyway). Cap offers within the owner's limits. 5. Write a win-back sequence (for example at 30, 60 and 90 days) built on genuine improvements, respecting unsubscribes. 6. Prototype the flow with app_build for review. 7. Flag auto-renewal and cancellation laws for the markets served (for example US state automatic-renewal laws, ROSCA, and UK and EU consumer rules; current requirements found with web_search) for counsel to confirm. 8. Set metrics: save rate by reason, 90-day retention of saved customers and complaint rate. 9. State what could not be verified: save-rate assumptions and legal requirements by jurisdiction.

skills.name: Public review responses
skills.one_liner: Reply drafts to Google, Yelp or marketplace reviews on-voice and on-policy.
skills.description: Drafts on-voice, on-policy replies to public reviews on Google, Yelp or marketplaces. Praise is thanked specifically and with varied wording. Complaints are acknowledged without disclosing private details or arguing, and moved offline. Suspected fake reviews get a platform flag rather than a public accusation. Replies are posted only after owner approval, with receipts.
skills.when: new reviews arrive, especially negative ones, or the review profile has gone unanswered

inputs.label: New reviews with rating, date and any linked order
Voice and tone guide
Sector-specific limits (health, legal or financial services)
Anything the owner knows about specific reviews

outputs.name: Review reply drafts
outputs.description: One reply per review, varied and specific.

outputs.name: Review summary and flags
outputs.description: Themes this week, suspected fake reviews with flag reports, and items for the owner.

skills.instructions: 1. Pull new reviews from connected profiles with connector_read (or the owner's pasted text), with rating, date and any linked order. 2. Classify each review: praise, mixed, complaint, suspected fake, or policy-violating. 3. Praise: thank them specifically (name what they liked), keep it brief and vary the wording; never copy and paste. 4. Complaints: acknowledge and apologise for the experience. Never confirm private details (health, order contents, staff names) or argue the facts in public. Say what's changing if the complaint is valid, and invite contact through a business channel. 5. Regulated sectors: a healthcare practice must never confirm that someone is a patient, and legal or financial services avoid discussing matters. Route those replies to the owner. 6. Suspected fake or policy-violating reviews: draft a platform flag report with reasons, and never accuse the reviewer publicly. 7. Never offer incentives to change or remove reviews, and never write reviews. 8. Batch the replies for approval with request_owner_decision; post with publish_external only after approval, keeping a receipt per reply. 9. State what could not be verified: whether each reviewer is a real customer.

workflow.acceptance: First line is APPROVED or CHANGES; no private details disclosed; no arguments; replies vary.

workflow.title: Owner approves replies

workflow.acceptance: Decision recorded per reply.

workflow.title: Post approved replies
workflow.brief: Post only approved replies through the connector.
workflow.acceptance: Only approved replies posted; a receipt per reply.

quality_checks.criterion: No private or protected details are disclosed (for example confirming someone is a patient)
Never offers incentives to change or remove reviews
